question_details.title: Will the President’s Malaria Initiative program cease to exist before January 1, 2026?
question_details.description:
This question is synced with an identical question on Metaculus. The original question opened on 2025-02-26 11:59:00 and can be found [here](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/35512). This question will resolve to the same value as the synced question. The original question's background info at this time is below. 

According to its Wayback Machine [January 17, 2025 archive](https://web.archive.org/web/20250117222410/https://www.pmi.gov/), the President’s Malaria Initiative (PMI) is described as follows: 

> The U.S. Government’s focal point for the global fight against malaria, the U.S. President’s Malaria Initiative has helped save millions of lives and contributed to substantial gains in education, productivity, and economic development.

> PMI started as a five-year initiative with the goal of reducing malaria deaths by 50% in 15 African countries. Thanks to the bipartisan support of Congress and the generosity of the American people, PMI now works in 27 partner countries in sub-Saharan Africa and three programs in the Greater Mekong Subregion in Southeast Asia–representing about 90% of the global malaria burden.

At the time of this question, its [website](https://www.pmi.gov/) showed the following error message: 

![](https://cdn.metaculus.com/user_uploaded/Screenshot_2025-02-23_at_8.31.12%C3%A2PM.png)

Created in 2005 [under President George W. Bush](https://georgewbush-whitehouse.archives.gov/infocus/malaria/), PMI [has been credited with](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5697814/) saving appoximately 940,000 lives in the 2005-2017 time period, mainly in Subsaharan Africa and the Greater Mekong Subregion of Southeast Asia.

On January 20, 2025, newly-inaugurated President Donald J. Trump signed Executive Order 14169 Reevaluating and Realigning United States Foreign Aid, which [targeted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_14169#USAID) in particular USAID, which operates the PMI program.

According to the [Kaiser Family Foundation](https://www.kff.org/policy-watch/the-status-of-president-trumps-pause-of-foreign-aid-and-implications-for-pepfar-and-other-global-health-programs):

> Despite the emergency humanitarian waiver specifying life-saving medicine and medical services, it was still unclear what programs it actually applied to and whether it included services provided by PEPFAR, the President’s Malaria Initiative, and other health programs, since under the State Department’s [framework for foreign aid](https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R40213), health programs and humanitarian assistance efforts are categorized separately. As a result, the PEPFAR program applied for a specific waiver, which was [granted on February 1](https://docs.google.com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vQgNTpC6F5oaOnkebQokJ_2eYgM_IcQNT7alIL6R3P16Ef4Z0pmQby3Y1eHbJcTxK_yJ8EPVNiibxON/pub), for certain activities. No other waivers have been announced for any other U.S. global health program, such as for the President’s Malaria Initiative (PMI), TB, maternal and child health, and nutrition activities.

As of February 23, 2025, USAID [was beginning](https://apnews.com/article/usaid-trump-musk-foreign-aid-firings-a3af8ce6ef17878b718c8e2ed3bf98e4) a round of mass layoffs of thousands of staffers, leaving the future of programs such as PMI in doubt.

question_details.resolution_criteria:
This question resolves as **Yes** if the United States President's Malaria Initiative ([PMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President%27s_Malaria_Initiative)) ceases to exist before January 1, 2026. This can come about through any of the following mechanisms:

* the initiative being terminated.
* the initiative and/or its functions merging with or being consolidated into another program or agency, with PMI no longer continuing to operate as a distinct organization.
* the program having its public funding eliminated by Congress.
question_details.fine_print:
* Because PMI was created by law, an enacted law that satisfies one of the above requirements would resolve the question as **Yes** immediately. In the event a presidential action would satisfy the above, the question will resolve as **Yes** if the action has taken effect for 60 consecutive days without being stayed, blocked, or otherwise halted by a federal court. In the event a presidential action is temporarily blocked by a court but later goes into effect for 60 days the question will resolve as **Yes**. The 60 day period must complete before January 1, 2026.
* Partial termination or partial elimination of funding is not sufficient.
* PMI being renamed will not count, as long as the core mission of funding global control of malaria remains intact within the same program.

Forecasters analyzing whether the President’s Malaria Initiative (PMI) will cease to exist before January 1, 2026, offered a diverse set of probabilities and reasoning, reflecting substantial uncertainty amid a historic foreign aid overhaul under the Trump administration. 

Three experts (Political Science – Punctuated Equilibrium, Advocacy Coalition Approach, and Global Health Policy) assign a high probability (78%, 85%, and 92%) that PMI will cease to exist. They emphasize the unprecedented executive actions: dissolution of USAID, transfer of PMI functions to the State Department, cancellation of most contracts, severe staff layoffs, and the disappearance of PMI’s distinct public identity (e.g., website offline). They point to the administration’s intent to dissolve PMI as a standalone program and argue that the ongoing situation may satisfy the fine print for cessation through legal termination, merger, or operational shutdown for the required 60 days. The weakening of advocacy coalitions, absorption of functions, and near-total operational shutdown are all seen as evidence that PMI is likely to end as a distinct entity before the resolution date. 

Other experts in the fields of International Development, Public Health, Global Health Governance, and African Studies are more cautious, assigning lower probabilities (25%, 12%, 30%, and 35%) of PMI ceasing to exist. While acknowledging the scale of the disruption and the executive branch’s objective to dismantle PMI, they stress key barriers: the legal and congressional inertia that typically protect Congressionally-authorized programs, continuation of at least some funding through continuing resolutions, persistence of the PMI brand or core mission as a technical entity (however diminished), and ambiguities as to whether a full legal or operational cessation has been conclusively realized under the fine print. Some highlight that humanitarian waivers and limited continuation of core activities indicate PMI has not fully ceased, and note the base rate for complete major U.S. health program abolition is very low, especially in such a short timeline. The experts in this camp expect that, despite severe disruption and moves toward consolidation, PMI may endure as a hollow or legally distinct shell through the deadline. 

In sum, there is consensus that the risk of PMI’s elimination is higher than ever due to aggressive executive action, operational shutdowns, and function transfers. However, a significant divide exists between those who believe the technical requirements for cessation will be met (favoring Yes, high probability) and those who see legal, congressional, and bureaucratic inertia preserving the minimal legal existence of PMI (favoring No, low-to-moderate probability). The forecasts thus range from a strong expectation of program cessation to a greater-than-usual, but still sub-50% risk of full elimination before January 1, 2026.
